To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the incidence of cancer in patients with venous thrombo-embolism ( VTE ) is 3.6% in patients with unprovoked VTE and (2) the risk of cancer is higher in men (5.3%) than in women (2.4%).
The prevalence of undiagnosed malignancy in idiopathic VTE patients was 3.4% (n = 11/325), and that the most common cancers were breast cancer (n = 3) and lymphoma (n = 2).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods and tools to support the diagnosis of cancer.
the development of new, effective and safe treatments for venous thrombo-embolism (deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism).
the study of the structure of the human body and its functions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk of VTE in cancer patients is increased and the treatment is more complex.
cancer patients with VTE should be treated in the same way as noncancer patients.
the risk of VTE in patients who have had cancer in the past is increased.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have a better understanding of the mechanisms of thrombosis and cancer and that the treatment of VTE in cancer patients is more complex than in those without.

the presence of cancer is an important risk factor for VTE, that the presence of VTE is an important risk marker for cancer, and that cancer patients have more complicated management of VTE than patients without cancer.

the diagnosis of idiopathic VTE should prompt a search for cancer, but the extent of the search should be individualized to the patient and should include the use of appropriate imaging studies and tumor markers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of cancer should not be a contraindication to anticoagulant therapy for VTE, and that anticoagulants can be used safely to treat cancer-associated VTE.
we should search for occult cancer in all patients with idiopathic venous thrombosis, but not all patients require extensive workup.
we should search for cancer aggressively, but we should be cautious about overdiagnosing and overtreating cancer.
